title: Visiting
hookLine: many Jews visit services unlike their own and learn from them

lines: A STRANGER POINTS TO THE LINE.
cards: A guest slips into the back row of a synagogue that isn't hers. Within five minutes she's lost. The melody for a prayer she has sung all her life is a different melody.
Nobody announces page numbers. Everyone stands at a moment she would have sat, and faces a direction she didn't expect. A kind stranger leans over and points to the line.
By the end she has learned a tune she'll hum for a week, and noticed something about her own synagogue she never saw from inside it.

teach.h: WHO IS WISE? WHO LEARNS FROM EVERYONE.
teach.b: Visiting. Four turns. First, the teaching behind it.
In the Mishnah, Ben Zoma asks: who is wise? The one who learns from every person. Not from every teacher: from every person.
A visitor walks in as a learner, the posture Ben Zoma calls wise. Second, what you might find. Some synagogues seat men and women apart, with a partition called a mechitza; some sit together.
Some pray almost entirely in Hebrew, quickly, each person at their own pace. Some sing slowly, in Hebrew and English, the whole room on one tune.
Sephardi and Ashkenazi rooms may chant the same words to different melodies. None of it is the visitor's to grade.
Each is somebody's home. Third, how to be a guest. Dress the way the room dresses.
Follow its lead: stand when it stands, keep your phone away where that's the custom.
Say less, watch more, and save your questions for afterward, over the cake, when people may be glad to explain.
Fourth, what comes home with you: a melody, a custom, a phrase, and your own synagogue, seen fresh, the way a trip abroad makes your own kitchen look new.
Hosts have their side too: hachnasat orchim, welcoming guests, a value the tradition traces to Abraham running from his tent to greet strangers.
A good visit needs a learner at the door and a welcome inside it.

how: Jews visit synagogues of other streams and styles while traveling, for a friend's celebration, or to learn, following the local customs of dress and seating and asking questions after the service.

o: inviting another congregation to your own
checking which synagogue does things correctly
going to another service as a learner and guest

p: the wise learn from every person
a partition between men and women

s: Ben Zoma says the wise learn only from great teachers
he says the wise learn from every person.
the same prayer can be sung to different melodies in different synagogues

games.q: you're a guest at an unfamiliar service. suddenly everyone stands and turns, and you don't know why. what do you do?
o: stay seated, since it isn't your custom.
stand with the room, and ask about it afterward.
leave quietly before you get it wrong again.
games.why: follow the room's lead and save the question for later: Ben Zoma's wise person is the one who learns from everyone.

practice: Think of a kind of service you've never been to, or not in years: another stream, another community, another style, maybe one a congregation streams online.
Choose one, and choose one thing to watch for when you go: a melody, a gesture, the way people greet each other at the door. If you pray, ask to be a good guest; if not, just hold the plan.

wordCard.voice: Visiting. Going to a service unlike your own as a learner and a guest, and coming home with something new. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: bringing in guests, the value of welcoming visitors.

carryVoice: Your line: visit. Every room you walk into is somebody's home, and you walk in as a learner. Go gently.
